findings.summary: The basics page ends with the fan-in merge goroutine and closer pattern, which use `close`, `sync.WaitGroup`, and a merge topology that the handbook never introduces.
findings.evidence: Page 1 blocks: "go func(c <-chan T) { // pass c: pre-1.22 / defer wg.Done() / for v := range c { out <- v } }(c) // spawned once per input channel" and "go func() { wg.Wait() // last producer finished / close(out) // nobody else knows when }()". `close` is first explained on page 7; `wg`/`WaitGroup`, `out`, and fan-in are never defined anywhere in the deck (the syllabus chapters "Fan-Out" and "Fan-In" have no pages).
findings.fix: Remove both code blocks from page 1 and place them on a Fan-In page after "Closing Channels", where `close`, the closer goroutine, and the WaitGroup are already established.

findings.summary: An entire page teaches `select` with `default` six pages before `select` itself is defined.
findings.fix: Delete page 2 and keep the try-receive where it already sits, in the select run (end of page 7 / page 8), so the reader meets `select` before its `default` clause.

findings.summary: Page 3 asserts closed-channel and nil-channel receive behaviour and the fan-out worker body before any of those are taught.

findings.summary: The unbuffered page opens by asserting that `close` broadcasts to every receiver, three pages before `close` is introduced.
findings.evidence: Page 4, "The Signal Channel": "done := make(chan struct{}) // 0 bytes" / "close(done) // wakes every receiver". Page 7 is where "`close(ch)` marks it closed" and "Close is a broadcast: it wakes every blocked receiver" are actually taught.
findings.fix: On page 4 show only `done := make(chan struct{})` plus the `done <- struct{}{}` / `<-done` completion signal that the page already uses, and keep the close-broadcast line for page 7.

findings.summary: The page calls `cap(ch)` racy, but a channel's capacity is fixed at `make` time and can never change.
findings.evidence: "`len(ch)` and `cap(ch)` are racy for decisions" / "The value can change before the next line runs"
findings.fix: Restrict the claim to `len(ch)`: "`len(ch)` is racy for decisions — it can change before the next line runs. `cap(ch)` is fixed at `make` time and is safe to read."

findings.summary: The runtime page teaches closed-channel receive semantics and the WaitGroup closer pattern before page 7 states the closing rules that motivate them.

findings.summary: "Every operation takes `hchan.lock` first" is false for `len`/`cap` and for the non-blocking fast path.
findings.evidence: "Every operation takes `hchan.lock` first"
findings.fix: Say "Every send, receive and close takes `hchan.lock` first" — `len(ch)`/`cap(ch)` read `qcount`/`dataqsiz` unlocked (which is exactly why `len` is racy), and `select` with `default` has a lock-free early-out when the channel is full/empty and open.

findings.summary: The claim that `make(chan T, n)` is a single allocation holds only when T contains no pointers; pointer-bearing element types get two allocations.
findings.evidence: "`make(chan T, n)` is one block: header plus `n*sizeof(T)`"
findings.fix: Qualify it: "`make(chan T, n)` is one block (header plus `n*sizeof(T)`) when T holds no pointers; if T contains pointers the runtime allocates `hchan` and `buf` separately." (runtime.makechan: the `elem.PtrBytes == 0` case is the only one that fuses them.)

findings.summary: "100k blocked goroutines cost KB" understates the memory by roughly five orders of magnitude.
